title: Ogbogu Okonji & Etiti Okonji: The Musical Partnership That Defined an Era of Ibusa Traditional Music
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
categories: Otu Ife Onye Lolu Nwa Nmadu
contentHtml:
Ogbogu Okonji & Etiti Okonji: The Musical Partnership That Defined an Era of Ibusa Traditional Music


As one who began listening to Ibusa traditional music as far back as the late 1970s, and as an Ibusa music enthusiast who has written extensively on the people’s rich tradition of traditional music, I would say that there is something particularly fascinating about the musical partnership between Ogbogu Okonji and his cousin, Etiti Okonji.

 

They were not simply two related musicians who happened to perform together; their collaboration was deeply rooted in childhood, family, Ibusa, and the broader tradition of Anioma indigenous music. Perhaps the most important aspect of their chemistry is that their musical relationship was not manufactured for a recording contract. They learned the tradition together, performed together, and developed their musical instincts from childhood.

 

Together, as paired vocalists in **Otu Ife Onye Lolu Nwa Nmadu**, they gave the Enuani some of their finest traditional music. Sadly, their partnership came to an end just when their combined artistry seemed poised to be fully appreciated and explored.

 

There is, therefore, much more to the story of Ogbogu Okonji and Etiti Okonji than their being cousins or musical partners. Their story is an important chapter in the history of Ibusa traditional music and in the evolution of the distinctive musical culture of the Enuani people.

 

Wait for Pen Master - Emeka Esogbue's forthcoming article on Ibusa musical pairs, with particular attention to Ogbogu Okonji and Etiti Okonji and their legendary group, Otu Ife Onye Lolu Nwa Nmadu.

title: ISM Alumni Network Announces Omu of Ibusa, Obi Josephine Nwannabuogwu, as Grand Matron
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
ISM Alumni Network Announces Omu of Ibusa, Obi Josephine Nwannabuogwu, as Grand Matron




By Emeka Esogbue


The newly established ISM Alumni Network (ISM Network) has announced HRH Obi Josephine Isioma Nwannabuogwu, the Omu of Ibusa, as its Grand Matron. The announcement followed the inaugural meeting of members of the association.


Members who spoke at the inaugural meeting expressed their appreciation for the choice of the Omu. Among them were Mrs. Ann Oligbo and Nneka Rosemary Eshiokwu.


Seconding the motion for the appointment, Nneka Eshiokwu said Omu Josephine Nwannabuogwu possesses the good spirit and qualities required to bring people together and mobilise them towards advancing the common good of Ibusa.


Mrs. Oligbo, on her part, described the choice of the Omu as a further promotion of Ibusa culture. She particularly noted that the Omu is blessed with a strong spirit of welfare and concern for the wellbeing of others.


The Omu of Ibusa was consequently adopted as the Grand Matron of the ISM Alumni Network.


Obi Josephine Isioma Nwannabuogwu was a former member and Welfare Officer of the Ibusa Singles Meet Worldwide.


Meanwhile, the Network is expected to formally present the Omu to Mrs. Rosemary Moji Ikolodo, Grand Matron of Ibusa Singles Meet Worldwide, the parent organisation of the Network; Mrs. Florence Agoh and Lady Benedicta Okonji, the Lagos and Ibusa Matrons respectively; and Dr. Prisca Okeleke, the group's Career Counsellor, for official recognition.


The Network's President, Ifeyinwa Izegbu, confirmed the planned presentation.

title: ISM Alumni Network Unites, Takes Off
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
ISM Alumni Network Unites, Takes Off



By Emeka Esogbue


Former members of the Ibusa Singles Meet Worldwide (ISM) have formed the ISM Alumni Network (ISM-Network), a new platform aimed at sustaining the bonds of friendship and community service established during their years in the group.


The ISM-Network currently comprises more than 80 members, all of whom have ancestral ties to Ibusa. While the current membership is drawn from a selection of former ISM members, other past members interested in joining the network are expected to indicate interest for membership.


At its inaugural general meeting, the group formed an executive body headed by Ifeyinwa Izegbu as President, with Victor Onwuka as Vice President, Mrs. Joyce Ifesindi as the General Secretary and other executive members.


The meeting also outlined several objectives for the new organisation. These include maintaining the friendships formed during the Ibusa Singles Meet years, organising social gatherings and reunions to keep members connected, undertaking charitable and community development projects in Ibusa, and promoting personal and family development through talks, seminars and other activities.


The network has also established a Welfare Department headed by Anthony Morha, which is expected to play a key role in promoting the wellbeing of members.


The ISM Alumni Network, a sister organisation of the Ibusa Singles Meet, is expected to contribute to the social development of the Ibusa community through its activities and collective initiatives.


The Ibusa Singles Meet Worldwide (ISM), Ibusa community's foremost singles groups, was founded by Emeka Esogbue, the author of this report, with the objective of bringing together singles of Ibusa extraction. The group also promotes marriage among Ibusa people.


According to records from the group, 44 members have so far married through relationships formed within the ISM, with the most recent marriage celebrated in 2025.


With the emergence of the alumni network, former members of ISM now have a dedicated platform to sustain the friendships, social connections and community-oriented values developed during their years in the singles group.

Past members of the Lagos Branch of ISM on a recreational visit

title: My Mother's Presence Encouraged Me, Merylin Ajidua, Ibusa Girl Who Won the Miss Earth Nigeria 2026 Model of the Year
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
My Mother's Presence Encouraged Me, Merylin Ajidua, Ibusa Girl Who Won the Miss Earth Nigeria 2026 Model of the Year



 *She contested in Miss Earth Nigeria and won the first Model of the Year Prize. She is grateful to all that supported her. Ibusa-born MISS MERYLIN IFESINACHI AJIDUA, in this interview with PEN MASTER (EMEKA ESOGBUE), shares her experience of the pageant in this interview. Excerpts:* 


 *Pen Master: Miss Merylin Ajudua, you just competed in Miss Earth Nigeria and returned with 2026 Model of the Year. Congratulations to you. Anyway, our readers will like to know you.* 



Ajidua: My name is Merylin Ifesinachi Ajidua. I am a humanitarian, environmental advocate, social entrepreneur, model, and the founder of the Merylin Ajidua Foundation, an NGO focused on youth empowerment, education, and community development. I am currently studying Educational Psychology, Guidance and Counselling at the University of Port Harcourt. I am passionate about using my voice and platforms to inspire young people, serve my community, and contribute meaningfully to environmental sustainability. I am also proudly the first ever Model of the Year at the just concluded Miss Earth Nigeria 2026 peagent. A title I am deeply grateful for. I am a Nigerian, from Umuafene, Isieke in Ibusa community, Delta State


 *Pen Master: Anyway, you just emerged the 2026 Model of the Year in  that pageant. How was the feeling like upon the announcement?* 


Ajidua: (Smile) Honestly, it was an emotional moment for me. When my name was announced, I felt a mixture of shock, gratitude, and happiness. I immediately thought about the little girl who had always dreamed of being on a stage like that. I thought about the doubts, the challenges, the preparation, and all the moments when I had to encourage myself to keep going. Being crowned Model of the Year made me realize that every step of the journey had a purpose. It wasn’t just a title to me. It felt like a reminder that dreams can actually become reality when you keep believing and showing up. 



 *Pen Master: What was running in your heart all through the contest?* 


Ajidua: Thank you Pen Master, but honestly, what was running in my heart throughout the contest was for God to let me become everything  I was there for. I came into Miss Earth Nigeria with a dream I had carried since I was a little girl, but I also came with fears and self-doubt. There were moments when I questioned myself, but I kept reminding myself why I started. I wanted to grow, to find my voice, to represent my values, and to use the platform to make a difference especially through my environmental advocacy. So even when things became challenging, my heart kept saying, keep going. You belong here. This is part of your story.” Today, becoming the 1st Ever Model of the Year makes me realize that every challenge, every tear, every correction, and every moment of doubt was preparing me for this moment. More than anything, my heart was filled with faith, gratitude, and the desire to make my little-girl dream a reality. 


 *Pen Master: ...but Merylin, what was the experience like for you?* 


Ajidua: The experience was honestly a beautiful mix of excitement, challenges, growth, and unforgettable memories. I came to Miss Earth Nigeria with a dream, but I quickly realized that the experience was about so much more than competing for a title. It challenged me to step outside my comfort zone, become more confident, find my voice, and learn how to carry myself with purpose. There were difficult moments too. There were times I doubted myself and wondered if I was doing enough, but those moments taught me resilience. My pageant sisters, my roommates, the team, and everyone who supported me became part of a journey I will always treasure. And emerging as the 1st Ever Model of the Year made the experience even more special. It reminded me that sometimes, the journey doesn’t look exactly how you imagined it, but it can still lead you to something beautiful. I didn’t just leave with a title. I left with growth, memories, friendships, confidence, and a stronger belief in myself. And for that, I will always be grateful.


 *Pen Master: This event was held in Port Harcout, the Garden City. Would you have wished it held in city outside Rivers State?* 


Ajidua: Yes, the event was held in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, and honestly, I’m grateful it was. I wouldn’t say I wished for it to be held somewhere else because Port Harcourt gave me an experience I will always cherish. The city welcomed us, and being there allowed us to experience its beauty, culture, and people. For me, the location was never the most important part. What mattered was the platform, the people I met, the lessons I learned, and the memories we created. That being said, I believe Miss Earth Nigeria is a national platform, and I would love to see future editions reach different cities across Nigeria. Taking the competition to different parts of the country could allow more young women to participate and showcase the beauty, culture, and environmental stories of their own communities. So, I wouldn’t replace Port Harcourt. I would simply love to see the Miss Earth Nigeria experience growth beyond it.


 *Pen Master: I observed that during the grand finale, your mother was physically present to watch you. She must be very fond of you.* 


Ajidua: (Laughing) Yes, my mother was the one who encouraged me to take the bold step. In her own words, “Dey here make your slimness dey waste" moved me to action. She is one of the people who has always been very special to me, so having her physically present at the grand finale meant so much to me. Seeing her there while I was on that stage was emotional because she wasn’t just watching the pageant, she was watching her daughter live out a dream. There is something very special about looking into the audience and seeing someone who has known you long before the crowns, makeup, gowns, and stage lights. Her presence gave me an extra sense of strength that night. Knowing that my mother was there to witness that moment is a memory I will treasure forever.


 *Pen Master: Alright, Merilyn, but what were the other girls always telling you in camp? Share their thoughts with us* 


Ajidua: (Smiling) my sisters were always encouraging me and reminding me to believe in myself. They would tell me things like, “Merylin, you can do this,” “Be confident,” “Don’t be afraid,” and sometimes they would even remind me to relax when I was taking things too seriously. I am grateful to my roommates I really appreciate Miss Lavender and Miss Primrose how they saw qualities in me that I sometimes couldn’t see in myself. We were competitors, but there were moments when we genuinely supported one another. That sisterhood is one of the things that made camp special for me.


 *Pen Master: Do you also model?* 


Ajidua: Yes, I do. Modeling has always been something I enjoy because it allows me to express myself through confidence, movement, fashion, and presence. My Miss Earth Nigeria experience also helped me understand that modeling is not just about appearance. It’s about confidence, discipline, expression, and the ability to communicate something without necessarily saying a word. Being named Model of the Year has definitely encouraged me to take that part of my journey even more seriously.


 *Pen Master: Meryline, you are a student of Educational Psychology Guidance and Counseling at the university of Port Harcourt. How do you combine your education with modeling?* 


Ajidua: well, it takes discipline and proper time management. My education is very important to me because I believe knowledge gives you a stronger foundation for whatever platform you eventually stand on. Modeling and pageantry have taught me confidence, presentation, discipline, and communication, while my studies help me understand people, their emotions, behaviours, and development. I actually see them as complementary. Education strengthens my mind, while modeling gives me another avenue to express myself and connect with people.


 *Pen Master: You are the founder of Merilyn Ajudua Foundation, an initiative aimed at youth empowerment and education. Tell us about this initiative.* 


Ajidua: the Merylin Ajidua Foundation was born from my desire to serve and create opportunities for people, particularly young people who may not always have access to the support their need. The foundation focuses on areas such as youth empowerment, education, humanitarian support, and community development. I believe young people shouldn’t only be seen as the leaders of tomorrow. We are also contributors today, and when young people are given the right knowledge, opportunities, mentorship, and support, they can transform their communities. My vision is to build something that goes beyond me. A platform that creates meaningful impact and encourages young people to believe that their circumstances do not have to define their future.


 *Pen Master: What message do you have for your fellow youths out there especially, your Ibusa people?* 


Ajidua: I would tell young people: don’t be afraid to start small, and don’t allow where you are today to convince you that you cannot become who you dream of being. I know what it feels like to have a dream and also have moments of doubt. But sometimes, you have to take the first step even when you don’t have everything figured out. Believe in yourself, keep learning, remain consistent, and surround yourself with people who encourage your growth. And most importantly, don’t measure your journey by someone else’s timeline. Your story is yours. Keep showing up, keep becoming, and trust that the little steps you are taking today can become the foundation for something much bigger tomorrow.


 *Pen Master: Merylin, I must thank you for your time and also wish you well in your career.* 


Ajidua: Pen Master, thank you so much for having me. It has been a pleasure sharing my story and my experience.

I am truly grateful to the Miss Earth Nigeria Organization, the National Director, my beautiful pageant sisters, my family, and everyone who supported me throughout this journey. This experience has given me memories I will carry for a lifetime, and I hope my story reminds someone else that it is okay to dream, it is okay to start small, and it is never too late to believe in yourself. I send my gratitude back home to my Ibusa brothers and sisters and indeed, everyone who supported me. Thank you for the opportunity.

title: Ibusa: Umuafene Clan Celebrates New Yam Festival in Grand Style as Prof. Emeritus Esogbue Sends Goodwill Message
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Ibusa: Umuafene Clan Celebrates New Yam Festival in Grand Style as Prof. Emeritus Esogbue Sends Goodwill Message



By Emeka Esogbue


Members of the Umuafene Clan in Umueakea Quarters, Ibusa, Delta State, gathered in the community on Thursday to celebrate the New Yam Festival, known locally as Iwa Ji. Joined by friends and well-wishers of the clan, the elated sons and daughters of Umuafene performed the traditional Iwa Ji rites in grand style.


Members of the clan, including youths, were seen rejoicing, singing, dancing and exchanging felicitations as they celebrated the annual festival.



The impressive turnout was commended by the Diokpa of the clan, Prof. Emeritus Augustine Onwuyali Esogbue, NNOM, who told Pen Master in a telephone conversation that he was deeply impressed by the celebration.


Prof. Emeritus Esogbue, a retired long-serving NASA scientist and Safety Advisory Board Medal recipient, is also the first Black person to be promoted to full professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology (Georgia Tech) and the first Black person to earn a Ph.D. in Industrial and Systems Engineering.


Commenting on the celebration, the renowned scholar said:


“I just saw the video accounts of the celebration of the 2026 Umuafene Iwa Ji Festival. It was highly successful. I have never seen anything like this before, at least, in our Umuafene Village.”


He added:


“My joy and gratitude go to all those who played a central role in making this day happen, and making it happen so successfully,”


the Ozorkilolo of Ibusa said.


“I am delighted that our people joined other communities to participate in this annual festival of our forefathers. I am grateful to everyone who made it happen,” he added.


The New Yam Festival is a communal expression of gratitude for life and harvest, as well as a celebration of unity and togetherness. It marks the end of one agricultural cycle and the beginning of another, while expressing hope for continued prosperity and a bountiful harvest in the coming season.


The people of Ibusa have, since time immemorial, celebrated the festival as an important part of their cultural heritage and communal life.


The Diokpa of Umuafene Clan, Prof Emeritus Esogbue also used the occasion to reiterate his plans to reconstruct the Umuafene Ogwa and conduct the Ikpota rites before the end of 2026.

title: 5 Energetic Dances of the Nigerian People
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
5 Energetic Dances of the Nigerian People


By Emeka Esogbue



Nigeria is a country richly blessed with diverse ethnic groups, each with its own distinctive cultural heritage, traditions, music, and dance forms. Across the country, traditional dances serve as powerful expressions of identity, communal life, history, celebration, and social values. Many of these dances are energetic, colourful, and captivating, combining rhythmic footwork, expressive body movements, coordinated gestures, traditional music, and elaborate costumes.


Performed during festivals, weddings, traditional ceremonies, title-taking ceremonies, cultural gatherings, and other important occasions, these dances provide entertainment while also preserving cultural knowledge and strengthening community bonds. They offer a window into the character, creativity, and social life of the communities that perform them.



This compilation highlights five energetic dances associated with different Nigerian ethnic communities, showcasing the remarkable cultural diversity and dynamism of the Nigerian people.


1. Gbagyi Dance


The Gbagyi (Gwari) people are an indigenous ethnic group in central Nigeria, particularly associated with the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja), Niger State, Kaduna State, and neighbouring areas. They possess a rich cultural heritage expressed through their language, farming traditions, arts, music, festivals, and dance.



Dance occupies an important place in Gbagyi communal life. Traditional dances are performed during celebrations, festivals, marriages, cultural ceremonies, and other important gatherings. Through music and movement, dancers express joy, communal solidarity, cultural pride, and a strong sense of identity. These performances also provide an important means of transmitting cultural knowledge from one generation to another.


Gbagyi dance is generally lively, rhythmic, and communal, with dancers responding to the beat of traditional drums and other musical instruments. Performers may dance in groups, using coordinated footwork, rhythmic stepping, bending, swaying, hand gestures, and expressive body movements. The dancers' movements often correspond closely with the rhythm and character of the accompanying music.


The combination of rhythmic movement, music, colourful traditional attire, and group participation makes Gbagyi dance an engaging expression of the community's cultural heritage.


2. Enuani Dance


The Enuani are one of the subgroups of the Anioma people of Delta North, Delta State. Major Enuani communities include Asaba, Ibusa, Ogwashi-Uku, Issele-Uku, Ubulu-Uku, Okpanam, and several other communities in the region.


The Enuani people have a distinctive cultural heritage expressed through language, traditional institutions, festivals, music, dance, marriage ceremonies, and communal celebrations. Their traditional dance culture includes forms known as Egwu Ohuhu or Egwu Oshushu, which are associated with rhythmic and expressive movement.


Enuani dance is characterised by rhythmic footwork, graceful body movements, coordinated group formations, and expressive gestures, with particular attention often given to movements of the waist and hips. Depending on the particular performance and social context, some movements may appear sensual or suggestive, particularly through hip-swaying and expressive body movements.


The dance is often performed communally, with dancers responding to traditional songs and percussion. The interaction between dancers, musicians, and spectators creates an atmosphere of celebration and social engagement.


Traditional clothing such as Akwa-Ocha, together with beads and colourful accessories, can further enhance the visual appeal of the performance. Beyond entertainment, Enuani dance represents cultural identity, communal unity, joy, social interaction, and respect for tradition. It remains an important means through which Enuani cultural values and artistic expressions are celebrated and passed on to younger generations.


3. Ikwerre Dance


The Ikwerre people are an indigenous ethnic group in Rivers State, southern Nigeria, particularly concentrated in and around areas such as Port Harcourt, Obio-Akpor, Ikwerre, and Emohua. The Ikwerre have a rich cultural heritage expressed through their language, traditional institutions, festivals, music, dance, marriage ceremonies, and communal life.


Dance occupies an important place in Ikwerre cultural celebrations. Traditional dances are performed during festivals, weddings, title ceremonies, cultural celebrations, and other community gatherings. They provide opportunities for people to celebrate their heritage while reinforcing social relationships and communal identity.


Ikwerre dance is generally lively, energetic, rhythmic, and communal. Dancers perform coordinated footwork, body movements, hand gestures, and rhythmic steps in response to traditional drums and other musical instruments. Men and women may participate in group performances, sometimes forming lines, circles, or other coordinated arrangements.


The dancers' movements may range from controlled and graceful gestures to more vigorous steps, depending on the particular dance and occasion. Traditional clothing, beads, ornaments, and other cultural accessories can add colour and visual splendour to the performance.


More than a form of entertainment, Ikwerre dance serves as a means of expressing cultural identity, celebrating communal life, preserving tradition, and strengthening unity. Its combination of music, movement, costume, and group participation makes it a vibrant component of Ikwerre cultural expression.


4. Owerre Dance



The Owerre people are an indigenous Igbo community associated particularly with Owerri and its surrounding areas in Imo State, southeastern Nigeria. The name Owerre is closely connected with the historical identity and origin of Owerri, the capital of Imo State.


The Owerre people possess a rich cultural heritage expressed through their language, traditional institutions, festivals, farming traditions, marriage customs, music, dance, and communal celebrations. As with many Igbo communities, traditional gatherings provide important occasions for music and dance.


Owerre dance is generally lively, rhythmic, expressive, and communal. Dancers use coordinated footwork, graceful body movements, hand gestures, and rhythmic swaying while responding to the beat of traditional drums and songs. Performances may involve groups of dancers moving together, creating a visually engaging display of coordination and cultural expression.


A notable feature of the dance is the interaction between the dancers and the audience. Female dancers, in particular, may use smiles, facial expressions, hand gestures, and other expressive movements while responding to the accompanying songs and rhythms. These expressions can contribute to the welcoming and sociable character often associated with communal Owerre celebrations.


Traditional attire, beads, and other cultural ornaments can further enhance the beauty and colour of the performance. Owerre dance therefore represents more than physical movement: it is a celebration of identity, hospitality, joy, social interaction, and communal pride.


5. Swange Dance of the Tiv


The Tiv people are one of the major ethnic groups of central Nigeria. Their traditional homeland is largely in Benue State, with Tiv communities also found in parts of Nasarawa, Taraba, Plateau, and Cross River states.


The Tiv have a distinctive cultural heritage expressed through their language, farming traditions, food, festivals, marriage customs, music, dance, and social institutions. Among the best-known expressions of Tiv cultural life is Swange, a lively traditional dance and musical form.


Swange is characterised by energetic, rhythmic, and expressive body movements, with particular emphasis often placed on coordinated hip and waist movements. Dancers respond closely to the rhythm of the accompanying music, creating a performance that is both visually engaging and highly communal.


Swange is especially captivating when performed by a group of dancers, as the coordinated movements create a strong sense of rhythm, unity, and visual harmony. The dancers may move in formation while maintaining individual expressions and movements, producing a lively interaction between music, dance, and spectators.


The dance is performed at social gatherings, celebrations, festivals, cultural events, and other important occasions. Beyond entertainment, Swange serves as an important expression of Tiv identity and cultural pride. It demonstrates the community's appreciation of music, movement, social interaction, and collective celebration.


Conclusion



The five dances discussed above demonstrate the extraordinary diversity and vitality of Nigeria's cultural heritage. From the rhythmic movements of the Gbagyi to the expressive traditions of the Enuani, the communal energy of Ikwerre and Owerre dances, and the lively movements of Tiv Swange, each dance tells a story about the people who created and preserved it.


These dances are not merely forms of entertainment. They are living expressions of identity, history, community, celebration, and cultural continuity. As Nigeria continues to evolve, preserving and promoting these traditional dances remains important because they connect younger generations with the cultural heritage of their ancestors while introducing Nigeria's rich traditions to the wider world.

title: Lost to Time: The Day Ibusa Celebrated Miss Ibusa
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Lost to Time: The Day Ibusa Celebrated Miss Ibusa




By Emeka Esogbue


On Friday, June 23, 2017, a youth event brought the people of Ibusa together in a remarkable way. It was the Miss Ibusa Pageant, organised by the National Association of Ibusa Students in conjunction with the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the Delta State Governor on Youth Development. Former Miss Kate Ifeyinwa Igbodo, CEO of Yinkee Entertainment and organiser of Miss Teen Anioma, served as the consultant for the event.


Ibusa was rarely known to come together in such a manner for youth-oriented events, apart from the annual Ibusa Football Tournament. The pageant, however, appeared to break that jinx.


The Nkata venue, also known as the Diokpa Palace, was filled to capacity, with prominent sons and daughters of the community in attendance. One after another, the contestants filed out, displaying beauty, poise and confidence as they faced the audience, their smiles betraying a mixture of excitement and anticipation. The crowd waved enthusiastically at their favourite contestants, while the Nkata hall reverberated with applause and expressions of appreciation.


The judging panel comprised Emeka Esogbue, this writer, as Chief Judge, supported by Nollywood celebrity Chief Emeka Ani and Ngozi Odiwe, Deputy Manager of the Delta Broadcasting Corporation.


Among the prominent Ibusa personalities who graced the occasion anchored by Shuntee Olinma and Vincent Iwunor were Hon. Barr. Princess Patience Ajudua, then a member representing Oshimili North Local Government Area in the Delta State House of Assembly; Chief Amaechi Nwaenie, the Uwolo of Ibusa; Dr. Austin Izagbo, then President-General of the Ibusa Community Development Union Worldwide; the late Mr. Frank Odita, former Commissioner of Police and Police Spokesperson; and Philip Ngozi Kwusike, the late novelist and writer, among several other distinguished personalities.


As speeches were delivered by various personalities, the atmosphere at the venue became even more charged. Rev. Fr. Paul Okobi, for instance, presented a paper on behalf of Rev. Fr. Frank Idayi, President of the Ibusa Indigenous Priests, Religious and Seminarians Association. The paper, titled “Ibusa Youth: General Appraisal (Causes and Effects of Their Restiveness),” addressed issues affecting the youth and their place in the development of the community.


But the climax of the occasion came with the announcement of Miss Juliet Olinma as the winner of the beauty contest. In line with the judges' decision, this writer, Emeka Esogbue, made the announcement.


The audience erupted in jubilation, with screams and cheers resonating throughout the venue. The excitement reached another level when Hon. Barr. Princess Ajudua crowned the new queen. The crowd went into a frenzy, and for a moment, the excitement seemed endless.


The pageant became the talk of the town.


But how far did the Ibusa youth event ultimately go?


With time, the idea of sustaining the beauty contest gradually faded away. The National Association of Ibusa Students, which organised the event, became almost unheard of. The young Ibusa women who had looked forward to wearing the crown someday saw their optimism dashed.


After Queen Juliet Olinma, there appeared to be no further opportunity for the community's pool of beautiful, intelligent and talented young women to compete for the crown, represent Ibusa and contribute to the community through meaningful projects.


The broader objective, essence and future envisioned for the event seem to have faded from the collective consciousness of the people.


Yet, PEN MASTER remains committed to digging into the history of the people, bringing forgotten moments back to the fore and reminding the present generation of events that once stirred the spirit of the community.


The Miss Ibusa Pageant may have been lost to time, but its memory remains a part of Ibusa's story.

title: Meet Onome Ezeka, the Young Akwa-Ocha Fabric Weaver
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Meet Onome Ezeka, the Young Akwa-Ocha Fabric Weaver



By Emeka Esogbue


Locating Onocity City, her weaving mill around the Ite-Ego axis within the Ibusa community felt like finding a living home of Akwa-Ocha, the cherished cultural fabric of the Anioma people.



Inside the modest weaving space, the rhythmic sounds of the looms filled the air. Young trainees, eager to master the craft, moved about with enthusiasm, smiling, welcoming customers and visitors, and attending to orders. It was more than a weaving mill; it was a place where culture was being preserved, one thread at a time.



At the centre of it all is Onome Ezeka, a young, vibrant woman who has turned her passion for Akwa-Ocha into a growing enterprise and a platform for teaching others.


I first met Onome in 2016 when she contested for Miss Teen Anioma, during my time as the Publicity Person. I celebrated with her when she emerged as the first runner-up.



Years later, I would meet her again but this time, in a completely different setting. Today, Onome is deeply involved in the production of Akwa-Ocha, weaving not only fabric but also a story of passion, identity and cultural continuity.


When I asked her how she got into the craft, her response was simple:


“I have always loved Akwa-Ocha for its purity and what it represents. For this reason, I went on to learn how to produce it. Even the one I wore for the 2016 pageantry was produced by me.”


That revelation says much about Onome’s journey. What began as an appreciation for the beauty and meaning of Akwa-Ocha gradually became a skill, and eventually, a vocation.


Today, she says she is living a dream she nurtured for years.


“Now, I have my dream come true after many years because I now have a personal place of my own where I produce and also train people on the production of the Anioma cultural fabric,” Onome told Pen Master.


Her weaving mill is therefore more than a place of production. It is also a training ground for young people who are learning the intricate craft and, in the process, becoming part of the continuing story of Anioma’s cultural heritage.


Onome says her services are affordable and that her products are tastefully finished to suit the preferences and needs of her customers. According to her, this attention to quality and customer satisfaction is one of the reasons many customers return after their first experience.


For Onome, however, the work goes beyond business.


It is about preserving something precious.


It is about keeping the threads of Anioma identity firmly in the hands of a new generation.


And as her young trainees gather around the looms, learning to turn threads into the beautiful patterns of Akwa-Ocha, Onome Ezeka is quietly proving that culture does not have to live only in museums or memories.


Sometimes, it lives in the hands of a young woman who chooses to keep weaving.


You can choose to be Onome Ezeka's Akwa-Ocha customer. See poster for more details.

title: PEN MASTER BELIEVES IN IBUSA PEOPLE FROM THE VERY BEGINNING: SEE PHOTOS OF MERYLN
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
PEN MASTER BELIEVES IN IBUSA PEOPLE FROM THE VERY BEGINNING: SEE PHOTOS OF MERYLN


Pen Master has a way of believing in Ibusa people and their capacity from the very beginning—not only when they have made it and are already at the top of the ladder.




Encouragement, motivation, and support matter greatly in helping people climb that ladder. The eyes of the Ibusa community are always watching, cheering, and supporting every son and daughter who dares to break new ground.


Take a look at these beautiful photos of Marilyn Ifesinachi Ajidua, the proud Anioma daughter from Ibusa, at the pageant camp of Miss Earth Nigeria.


Beautiful Marilyn Ajidua is once again proving that Anioma people are never missing in action. We show up, we stand tall, and we make our presence felt wherever excellence calls.


Ibusa is watching. Anioma is proud. Keep shining, Marilyn!

title: A Son of Anioma Answers the Call: Rev. Morris Chukwunonso Mordi to Be Ordained
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
A Son of Anioma Answers the Call: Rev. Morris Chukwunonso Mordi to Be Ordained




Here, in the Catholic Archdiocese of Lagos, priestly and diaconate ordinations are taking place, and I trust you know that Anioma can never be missing—not with the abundance of human capital and vocations God has blessed us with. Yes, there must always be an Anioma!


Among those to be ordained is Rev. Morris Chukwunonso Mordi, a proud son of our Issele-Uku community.


Born on April 7, 1998, into the devout Catholic family of Mr. and Mrs. George Mordi, Morris initially planned to study Banking and Finance at Delta State University, Abraka. He sat for and passed the university’s Post-UTME examination and was subsequently offered admission.


However, as the date of resumption drew near, Morris received another admission letter, this time from the seminary through the Lagos Archdiocese. As he contemplated which path to follow, something remarkable happened: the admission letter from Abraka mysteriously disappeared without a trace.


Perhaps, in that moment, divine providence was at work.


Guided by faith and drawn to the childhood dream of dedicating his life to the service of God, Morris chose the seminary and answered the call to serve Christ and His Church through the Catholic priesthood.


Today, we celebrate not only a young man answering his vocation, but also a son of Anioma taking his place in the vineyard of the Lord.


Welcome to the priesthood, Rev. Morris Chukwunonso Mordi! 


Ezigbo nwa Oligbo Issele-Uku!


May God grant you wisdom, strength, grace and perseverance as you begin this sacred journey. May your priesthood be fruitful, holy and a blessing to many.


Anioma is proud of you!


- Emeka Esogbue

title: Anioma Watch Association Inaugurates Executive Officers as BoT Chairman, Emeka Esogbue, Urges Them to Lead with Integrity and Remain Accessible
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Anioma Watch Association Inaugurates Executive Officers as BoT Chairman, Emeka Esogbue, Urges Them to Lead with Integrity and Remain Accessible


By Peter Oshagwu


Anioma Watch Association on Tuesday inaugurated its newly appointed executive officers, formally presenting them to members of the Anioma nation at a ceremony held on Ezenei Avenue, Asaba, Delta State.


The event, which was described as historic by some attendees, marked a significant milestone in the development of the association, which was founded in 2022.


In his welcome address, the Chairman of the Board of Trustees, Dr. Emeka Esogbue, said the association had grown from a modest beginning into a vibrant platform united by a shared aspiration for a more cohesive Anioma.


Esogbue, who described Anioma Watch Association as more than an organisation of words and aspirations, said the group was committed to action, service and the advancement of the Anioma people.


He charged the newly inaugurated officers to lead with integrity, humility, transparency and courage, while remaining accessible to members and promoting unity rather than division.


“To the newly inaugurated executives, I offer my warmest congratulations and, at the same time, a solemn charge: you have been entrusted with the responsibility of building upon the foundation already laid and of giving fresh impetus to the vision and mission of Anioma Watch Association.


“You are expected to lead with integrity, humility, transparency and courage; to remain accessible to members; to promote unity rather than division; and to ensure that the interests of Anioma people remain at the heart of your decisions and programmes,” the Nigerian historian said.


He further urged the new executives to strengthen the association’s engagement with Anioma communities at home and in the diaspora, promote the culture and heritage of the people, expand charitable and humanitarian interventions, and remain vigilant in monitoring and advocating for their social, economic and political interests.


“You must strengthen our engagement with Anioma communities at home and in the diaspora, promote our culture and heritage with pride, expand our charitable and humanitarian interventions, and remain vigilant in monitoring and advocating for the social, economic and political interests of our people. You can only achieve these if you give your time and personal moments,” he said.


Esogbue also reminded the officers that their new positions were a call to service rather than an avenue for personal recognition.


“I urge you to see this mandate not as an opportunity for personal recognition, but as a sacred trust bestowed upon you by the Association and by the people whose interests we have pledged to serve.


“The road ahead may present challenges, but with dedication, teamwork, consultation and an unwavering commitment to the common good, I am confident that you will take Anioma Watch Association to a new level of relevance, impact and influence.”


In his acceptance speech, the newly appointed President of the organisation, Engr. Abela Emuebie Ihienkaegho, expressed his readiness to serve and pledged to contribute to the advancement of the Anioma people.


Ihienkaegho, a Senior Software Engineer, said Anioma Watch Association must emerge as a credible, courageous and unifying voice for the Anioma people, championing their economic prosperity, sustainable development, social wellbeing, cultural preservation and political progress.


“We must preserve our history, culture and traditions, and ensure that our heritage is properly documented for future generations,” he said.


The newly appointed officers were sworn in by Rev. Felix Ifeanyi Nwabuokei, the General Secretary of the Board of Trustees.


Other officers unveiled at the ceremony include Engr. Onyeabo Nwawo, Vice President; Mr. Peter Oshagwu, General Secretary; Mr. Awele Oranye, Assistant General Secretary; and Mrs. Tessy Joseph.


Others are Miss Ifeyinwa Izegbu, Treasurer; Miss Joy Ozeh; Miss Eunice Emeyazia; Chief Dr. Macdonald Okonkwo, Ex-Officio; and Mr. Patrick Obi, Ex-Officio.


Anioma Watch Association was founded in 2022, while the newly inaugurated executive officers will serve a two-year tenure.

title: WELCOME ADDRESS BY THE CHAIRMAN, BOARD OF TRUSTEES, ANIOMA WATCH ASSOCIATION, DR. EMEKA ESOGBUE, AT THE INAUGURATION CEREMONY OF THE EXECUTIVE OFFICERS OF THE ASSOCIATION
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
WELCOME ADDRESS BY THE CHAIRMAN, BOARD OF TRUSTEES, ANIOMA WATCH ASSOCIATION, DR. EMEKA ESOGBUE, AT THE INAUGURATION CEREMONY OF THE EXECUTIVE OFFICERS OF THE ASSOCIATION


 

Date: September 1, 2026 


Venue: Asaba, Delta State

 

Protocols duly observed.

 

Distinguished guests, members of the Board of Trustees, esteemed leaders and stakeholders of Anioma, our newly inaugurated Executive Officers, members of the Anioma Watch Association at home and in the diaspora, ladies and gentlemen, it is with great joy, humility and a deep sense of responsibility that I welcome you all to this historic occasion. Today, September 1, 2026, marks another significant milestone in the journey of Anioma Watch Association, an organisation founded in 2022 with a clear commitment to projecting the interests of Anioma people, promoting our rich culture and heritage, and fostering unity among our people. 


Over the years, the Association has grown from its modest beginnings into a vibrant platform, including a thriving WhatsApp community of over one thousand members, united by a common aspiration for a stronger, more prosperous and more cohesive Anioma. In pursuit of our mission to watch over the social, economic and political interests of Anioma and to extend a helping hand to the vulnerable through charitable interventions, we have recorded commendable milestones, including the organisation of the Anioma Legacy Lecture in Asaba, anti-drug abuse programmes in secondary schools across Anioma, and, most recently, an antenatal outreach programme through which new-life starter packs were presented to expectant mothers in five Anioma communities. 


These achievements demonstrate that Anioma Watch Association is not merely an organisation of words and aspirations; it is an organisation committed to action, service and the advancement of our people. It is therefore against this background of shared vision, service and collective responsibility that we gather today to inaugurate a new team of Executive Officers who will be entrusted with the responsibility of taking this noble mission to even greater heights.


As we inaugurate these Executive Officers today, we must recognise that leadership is not a title or position of privilege, but a call to service, sacrifice and accountability. To the newly inaugurated executives, I offer my warmest congratulations and, at the same time, a solemn charge: you have been entrusted with the responsibility of building upon the foundation already laid and of giving fresh impetus to the vision and mission of Anioma Watch Association. You are expected to lead with integrity, humility, transparency and courage; to remain accessible to members; to promote unity rather than division; and to ensure that the interests of Anioma people remain at the heart of your decisions and programmes. 


You must strengthen our engagement with Anioma communities at home and in the diaspora, promote our culture and heritage with pride, expand our charitable and humanitarian interventions, and remain vigilant in monitoring and advocating for the social, economic and political interests of our people. You can only achieve these if you give your time and personal moments. I urge you to see this mandate not as an opportunity for personal recognition, but as a sacred trust bestowed upon you by the Association and by the people whose interests we have pledged to serve. The road ahead may present challenges, but with dedication, teamwork, consultation and an unwavering commitment to the common good, I am confident that you will take Anioma Watch Association to a new level of relevance, impact and influence.


CONCLUDING REMARKS


Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, as we celebrate this important day, let us remind ourselves that the strength of Anioma Watch Association lies not in the name of the organisation alone, but in the collective commitment of its members to the ideals that brought us together. Our diversity across communities and walks of life should be a source of strength, not division. We must therefore continue to build bridges across the Enuani, Ika, and Ndokwa, encourage constructive dialogue, support one another and work together in the best interest of Anioma.


To the new Executive Officers, I once again congratulate you on your inauguration. You have our support, our prayers and our goodwill. But above all, you have our expectations. May your two-year tenure be defined by meaningful programmes, responsible leadership, measurable achievements and a renewed sense of purpose. May you consolidate the gains already recorded by the Association and open new frontiers of service, advocacy, humanitarian intervention and community development.


As a Board of Trustees, we pledge our continued guidance and support to the executive, while also maintaining our commitment to the principles of accountability, transparency and service. We equally call upon every member of Anioma Watch Association to see this new chapter as a collective responsibility. There is a place for everyone in building the Anioma we desire, and every positive contribution, no matter how small, can make a difference.


Our Association has come a long way since its foundation in 2022. From providing a platform for dialogue and advocacy to reaching communities through education, health and humanitarian initiatives, we have demonstrated what can be achieved when people come together with a shared vision. The future, however, demands even greater commitment. We must continue to watch, speak, serve and act—not only when circumstances demand it, but as a continuing responsibility to our people and generations yet unborn.


We have many amongst us who have sacrificed their time, efforts and personal resources because they believe in this Association and the Anioma project as a whole. These people must never be let down. For more than two decades, I have shown personal commitments to the Anioma cause through historical research, and writings, spotlight of indigenes, projection of core civilizations, promotion of the people's cultural institutions and heritage and projection of the people to the world. These have come as sacrifices because of my personal belief that the region and its people deserve a place in global space. You may choose to do better than I have performed.


Let us therefore leave this ceremony with a renewed determination to make Anioma Watch Association an even stronger voice for Anioma, a dependable instrument for community development, a guardian of our cultural heritage and a platform that promotes unity, dignity and progress.


On behalf of the Board of Trustees, I warmly welcome you all once again and sincerely thank our distinguished guests, members, friends and supporters for honouring this occasion with your presence. May the newly inaugurated Executive Officers be blessed with wisdom, courage and the capacity to serve effectively. May Anioma continue to prosper in peace and unity, and may our collective efforts contribute meaningfully to the advancement of our people.


Long live Anioma Watch Association.


Long live Anioma people.


Long live the Federal Republic of Nigeria.


Thank you all, and God bless you.


Uwaoma nu!


Ogbueshi!


Ajie nu!

title: Anioma Watch Association Commends Onicha-Olona on the  Successful Enthronement of the Omu Institution
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
August 31, 2026


 *PRESS RELEASE* 


Anioma Watch Association Commends Onicha-Olona on the  Successful Enthronement of the Omu Institution 






The Anioma Watch Association, a socio-cultural organisation of the Anioma people at home and in the Diaspora, warmly congratulates the people of Onicha-Olona on the  successful enthronement of the Omu institution in the community. The Association considers this significant development a welcome reaffirmation of Onicha-Olona’s rich cultural heritage, traditional values, and enduring commitment to preserving institutions that promote unity, identity, and continuity for present and future generations.


We are particularly delighted that Onicha-Olona, one of Anioma’s foremost communities renowned for its rich cultural practices and one of the earliest Enuani communities in which the Omu institution was traditionally practised, has collectively chosen to revive this important cultural institution. This remarkable development underscores the resilience of the Anioma people and their determination to preserve, strengthen, and promote the cultural heritage and civilisation handed down through generations.


The Association is further delighted by the community’s choice of HRH Nwamaka Cynthia Jibunoh, as the newly installed 9th Omu of Onicha-Olona as a successor of HRH Justina Okukaleke Ntoka, the late Omu. We extend our heartfelt congratulations to her and wish her a peaceful, impactful, and successful reign as she assumes this important traditional responsibility.


The Association also acknowledges the growing role of the Omu institution in advancing community development and improving the wellbeing of the people. In this regard, we recall with great satisfaction the antenatal programme hosted on August 17, 2026, by HRH Obi Josephine Isioma Nwannabuogwu, the Omu of Ibusa, during which maternal items were presented to expectant mothers at a Primary Health Centre in the community.


We are pleased that our Association is able to leverage the Omu institution and other relevant traditional platforms across Anioma to support initiatives that directly touch the lives of our people and put smiles on their faces. We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to working with traditional institutions, community leaders, and other relevant stakeholders across Anioma in advancing initiatives that promote the welfare, development, and unity of our people.


Once again, the Anioma Watch Association felicitates with the people of Onicha-Olona on this important cultural accomplishment. We commend the community for this collective achievement and encourage its people to build on this milestone by pursuing further initiatives that strengthen their cultural identity, unity, and collective progress.


Long Live Onicha-Olona Kingdom!


Long Live Anioma Watch Association!


Long Live Anioma!


Long Live Delta State!
