title: Anioma Watch Association’s Antenatal Giveaway Draws Mammoth Turnout in Agbor
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Anioma Watch Association’s Antenatal Giveaway Draws Mammoth Turnout in Agbor






By Emeka Esogbue


A mammoth turnout of expectant mothers was recorded in Agbor as the Anioma Watch Association distributed essential antenatal items to pregnant women as part of its efforts to support maternal health and ease the financial burden associated with pregnancy.


The Anioma Watch Association team, on Thursday, took its antenatal outreach programme to Central Hospital, Agbor, in Delta State, where expectant mothers from the community received new-life packs containing essential items to support them during pregnancy and prepare them for childbirth.


The Anioma Watch team was warmly received by the Zonal Director of Central Hospital, Agbor, Dr. Grace Eseka, and Mrs. Okwudihu Patricia, Matron of the hospital. Dr. Eseka thanked the organisation for choosing the hospital as the venue for the outreach.


Speaking at the event, the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of Anioma Watch Association, Dr. Emeka Esogbue, thanked the expectant mothers for their presence and described Anioma Watch as a socio-political watchdog of the Anioma people.


Esogbue encouraged the women to raise their children to become responsible and productive members of the Agbor community, Anioma and Nigeria at large.


Also speaking, the Chairman and Media Director to the Delta State Governor, Mr. William Eghebi, commended Dr. Grace Eseka for her outstanding contributions to the management and development of hospitals in the community.


Eghebi urged the expectant mothers to raise their children to become better individuals and productive citizens in the future. He assured the group of his willingness to support its activities in any way possible, noting that while it might not be possible to meet every need, every form of assistance counts.


Engr. Abela Emuebie, in his remarks, advised the expectant mothers on proper nutrition and the importance of maintaining a healthy diet during pregnancy.


Founded in 2022, Anioma Watch Association is a registered socio-cultural organisation of the Anioma people. The current antenatal outreach project was facilitated by Dr. Anthony Ezeagbor, a member of the organisation’s Board of Trustees.

title: Emeka Esogbue: Historian, Journalist, and Voice of Anioma Culture
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
categories: A Study of the Origins and Migrations of Anioma Settlement
contentHtml:
Emeka Esogbue: Historian, Journalist, and Voice of Anioma Culture



By Roseline Uche Iwendi


Chukwuemeka Jerry Esogbue, widely recognized as “The Pen Master,” is a Nigerian historian, researcher, journalist, research editor, and cultural advocate whose work has contributed significantly to the documentation and preservation of Anioma history and cultural heritage.


Born on June 6, 1970, in Ibusa (Igbuzo), Oshimili North Local Government Area of Delta State, Esogbue has devoted decades to researching and documenting the history, identity, traditions, and experiences of the Anioma people.


Bridging Oral Tradition and Written History


One of the defining features of Esogbue’s work is his effort to bridge the gap between oral tradition and documented history. His research explores a wide range of subjects, including Anioma and Igbo origins, migrations, colonial encounters, traditional institutions, diplomacy, cultural practices, and the biographies of notable individuals.


His approach is distinctly hybrid, combining rigorous documentary research with extensive fieldwork. Through interviews, community engagement, archival investigation, and the collection of firsthand accounts, he seeks to preserve historical narratives that might otherwise remain undocumented or be lost with time.


This methodology has enabled him to bring together written records and community memories, creating a richer understanding of Anioma history from both documentary and indigenous perspectives.


The Pen Master Blog and Digital Documentation


Through his Pen Master Blog, Esogbue has taken Anioma and Ibusa history beyond local communities and into the global digital space. The platform has served as an extensive repository of cultural articles, interviews, historical essays, biographies, and research materials.


Its core areas of interest include Anioma and Igbo history, colonialism, traditional diplomacy, cultural identity, and regional biographies. By using digital media to document and disseminate historical knowledge, Esogbue has helped make local histories more accessible to researchers, students, members of the diaspora, and a wider international audience.


Journalism and Editorial Contributions


Beyond historical research, Esogbue has also established himself as a journalist and editor. His professional and editorial engagements have included roles such as Editor-at-Large of Integrity Watchword Magazine and Research Editor for Anioma Essence Magazine/OFAAC Media Associations and Homage Magazine.


These roles reflect the intersection of his interests in journalism, research, cultural advocacy, and historical documentation. Through them, he has continued to promote informed conversations about identity, heritage, society, and the historical experiences of the Anioma people.


Preserving a Cultural Legacy


Esogbue’s contribution extends beyond the recording of historical facts. Through his sustained chronicling of Anioma identity and heritage, he has helped transform localized memories and traditions into a globally accessible historical record.


By anchoring oral traditions in documentary research and modern digital media, “The Pen Master” has created a platform through which the legacy, achievements, struggles, and cultural nuances of his people can be preserved for present and future generations.


His enduring commitment to research, journalism, and cultural preservation may, indeed, be one of the reasons the name “The Pen Master” has become so closely associated with him.

title: ANIOMA WATCH TAKES MATERNAL CARE OUTREACH TO AMAI, AS EVANGELIST DORIS ABOH, HON. GABRIEL OSEH JOIN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
ANIOMA WATCH TAKES MATERNAL CARE OUTREACH TO AMAI, AS EVANGELIST DORIS ABOH, HON. GABRIEL OSEH JOIN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT 





By Emeka Esogbue


The Anioma Watch Association has taken its five-day maternal and child healthcare outreach to Amai in Ukwuani Local Government Area of Delta State, providing new-life starter packs and health education to expectant mothers at the community’s Primary Health Centre.


The outreach, held on Friday, brought together expectant mothers, healthcare workers, community representatives and members of the Anioma Watch Association, with prominent Amai personalities, including Evangelist Doris Aboh and Hon. Gabriel Oseh, among those who graced the event.


The programme commenced with an opening prayer by Miss Joy Ozeh, followed by the introduction of the Anioma Watch team by the association’s President, Engr. Abela Emuebie Ihienkaegho.


Welcoming the delegation, the Matron of the Primary Health Care Centre, Amai, Mrs. Benedicta Egwuenu, expressed delight over the turnout of expectant mothers and the selection of the facility for the outreach.


Egwuenu said the hospital maintained proper documentation of its patients, noting that she was familiar with many of them by name. She subsequently introduced members of the health facility’s staff.


The Special Guest of Honour, Evangelist Doris Aboh, who described herself as a proud daughter of Amai, said she preferred to regard herself as the host of the occasion and the Anioma Watch delegation as her guests.


Aboh, a Nigerian Christian evangelist and media professional who served as Senior Special Assistant on Media to former Delta State Deputy Governor Kingsley Otuaro during the Okowa administration, expressed excitement that the Anioma Watch initiative had extended to Amai.


Speaking on the theme, “Healthy Mothers, Healthy Children: The Place of Medical Care, Faith and Community Support,” Aboh described pregnancy as a beautiful journey that requires wisdom, attention and proper care.


She urged expectant mothers to combine faith with appropriate medical care, stressing that antenatal services should not be treated as optional.


According to her, pregnant women should register for antenatal care early and attend their appointments regularly, while also paying close attention to their health after childbirth.


Aboh called for a stronger culture of maternal support in Amai, where pregnant women would feel free to seek medical attention, husbands would actively support their wives to attend antenatal clinics, and families would work together to ensure that mothers receive the care they need.


She also appealed to traditional rulers, religious leaders, community leaders, philanthropists and other well-meaning sons and daughters of Amai to sustain support for maternal healthcare initiatives.


While commending the distribution of mother-and-child starter packs, she noted that such material assistance should be complemented by knowledge, access to quality healthcare, encouragement and sustained community support.


In his remarks, the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of Anioma Watch Association, Dr. Emeka Esogbue, described the organisation as a socio-cultural body committed to promoting societal development across the Anioma region.


Esogbue explained that the decision to take the outreach to Amai was informed by the association’s interest in the community and the encouragement of Chief Alfred Onyenwosa, the Onochieze of Amai.


He described mothers as “mothers of the nation” and encouraged the expectant women to prioritise their health so they could adequately care for their children.


The Anioma Watch trustee chairman further charged the women to raise children who would grow into responsible and productive citizens capable of contributing meaningfully to the development of Amai Kingdom and Nigeria.


He acknowledged the challenges associated with raising children, including sacrifice, patience and uncertainty, while encouraging the mothers to persevere and continue to pray for their families.


He expressed hope that the new-life starter packs provided by Anioma Watch would offer useful support to the beneficiaries during the early stages of motherhood.


Also speaking, Hon. Gabriel Oseh, a councillor from the community, conveyed the appreciation of the traditional ruler and the President-General of the Amai Development Union to Anioma Watch Association for selecting Amai for the initiative.


Oseh described the community as fortunate to be among those selected for the outreach and declared the entire Anioma Watch delegation indigenes of Amai.


The declaration was one of the highlights of the event, alongside a traditional Ukwuani welcome song performed by Mrs. Uti Florence in honour of the visiting delegation.


Other participants included Rev. Felix Nwabuokei, General Secretary of the Anioma Watch Association Board of Trustees; Miss Ifeyinwa Izegbu, Treasurer; Miss Joy Ozeh, Welfare/Social Secretary; and Miss Gloria Idegwu, a member of the association.


The health facility was represented by Mrs. Benedicta Egwuenu, Matron of Primary Health Care, Amai, and Mrs. Nze Vivian, Community Health Essential Worker.


The Amai outreach marked the conclusion of Anioma Watch Association’s five-day antenatal outreach programme, during which the organisation visited Ibusa, Issele-Uku, Onicha-Olona, Agbor and Amai.


At each location, the association provided new-life starter packs to expectant mothers while promoting maternal health awareness and the importance of community support for mothers and children.

title: Anioma Watch Extends Maternal Support to Expectant Mothers in Onicha-Olona
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Anioma Watch Extends Maternal Support to Expectant Mothers in Onicha-Olona


By Emeka Esogbue


The Anioma Watch Association has extended its community-based maternal support initiative to Onicha-Olo




na, Delta State, with the distribution of maternal starter packs to expectant mothers at the Onicha-Olona Primary Health Centre.


The outreach, which brought together expectant mothers and community leaders, was designed to provide essential items to women preparing for childbirth and the early care of their newborns. The initiative underscores Anioma Watch’s commitment to promoting maternal and child wellbeing and supporting families within Anioma communities.


The programme commenced early in the morning, with expectant mothers arriving at the health centre from about 7:00 a.m. The Matron of the facility, Mrs. Okoh Ewere, welcomed the Anioma Watch delegation and expressed appreciation to the association for selecting the health centre as a beneficiary of the intervention.


Welcoming the Anioma Watch team on behalf of the community, the President-General of the Onicha-Olona Development Union, Sir Patrick Anibuofu Ejidoh, described the maternal packs as a meaningful investment in the future of the community.


He noted that the children being carried by the expectant mothers represented the future leadership of the community and the nation, stressing the importance of initiatives that support mothers during pregnancy.


Ejidoh also commended Anioma Watch for mobilising resources to provide assistance to members of the public, observing that it was uncommon to find social organisations that consistently raise funds for such humanitarian interventions.


While acknowledging that the association could not provide everything mothers might need, he urged the beneficiaries to appreciate the support and make good use of the items provided.


In his opening address, the Chairman of the Anioma Watch Board of Trustees, Dr. Emeka Esogbue, described women as “mothers of the nation” and charged the expectant mothers to see parenting as a responsibility that extends beyond childbirth.


Esogbue emphasised that the ultimate goal should not only be to give birth to children but to raise responsible individuals who would contribute meaningfully to the development of Onicha-Olona, Anioma and Nigeria.


He urged the mothers to provide proper guidance and values for their children, noting that responsible parenting was critical to building a productive and progressive society.


The President of Anioma Watch, Engr. Abela Emuebie Ihienkaeghor, also advised the expectant mothers to pay close attention to their wellbeing and maintain healthy eating habits throughout pregnancy.


The outreach ended with a vote of thanks delivered by Dr. Miracle Nwanze, while Precious Onwueze led the closing prayer.


The maternal support programme adds to Anioma Watch’s growing community-focused interventions, highlighting the role of organised community groups in complementing existing efforts to improve the wellbeing of mothers, children and families.

title: Evangelist Doris Aboh Named Special Guest of Honour for Anioma Watch Maternal Care Outreach in Amai
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Evangelist Doris Aboh Named Special Guest of Honour for Anioma Watch Maternal Care Outreach in Amai



By Emeka Esogbue


Evangelist Doris Aboh, a prominent indigene of Amai Kingdom and Nigerian Christian evangelist, has been named Special Guest of Honour for the Anioma Watch Association’s maternal care and antenatal outreach programme in Amai, Delta State.


The announcement was contained in a statement made available in Asaba by the President of Anioma Watch Association, Chief Abela Emuebie Ihienkaeghor, alongside other prominent community leaders involved in the initiative.


The Anioma Watch Association, a registered socio-cultural organisation representing Anioma people at home and in the Diaspora, is currently implementing a maternal care programme aimed at supporting expectant mothers across selected Anioma communities.


Aboh’s appointment adds a notable community dimension to the Amai leg of the programme, as she is expected to attend the outreach and support the Association’s efforts to improve maternal and child welfare in the community.


Other community leaders have also been appointed to support the programme in their respective communities. Chief Angus Obima-Nwali 

and Chief Mrs. Rosemary Ibude, Oso Diya Eri are to participate in the Agbor edition, while Sir Patrick Anibuofu Ejidoh, President-General of the Onicha-Olona Development Union, has been named Special Guest for the Onicha-Olona outreach.


The programme has already reached communities including Ibusa and Issele-Uku. On Monday, the Omu of Ibusa, HRH Obi Josephine Nwannabuogwu, oversaw the outreach in Ibusa, where she advised expectant mothers to raise their children responsibly and nurture them to become productive contributors to community development.


At the Ibusa outreach, expectant mothers received maternal and child-care items intended to support them during pregnancy and after delivery.


The Association has so far visited the Primary Health Care Centre in Ibusa and Pilgrim Baptist Hospital in Issele-Uku, where maternal-care items were distributed to expectant women.


The outreach is expected to continue in Onicha-Olona, Agbor and Amai, with expectant mothers in the beneficiary communities scheduled to receive mother-and-child starter packs.


The initiative reflects the Association’s growing focus on community-based social interventions, particularly programmes designed to support mothers, children and vulnerable families across Anioma communities.

title: Pilgrim Baptist Hospital Trustees Applaud Anioma Watch for Maternal Care Outreach in Issele-Uku
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Pilgrim Baptist Hospital Trustees Applaud Anioma Watch for Maternal Care Outreach in Issele-Uku





By Peter Oshagwu


The Board of Trustees of Pilgrim Baptist Hospital, Issele-Uku, has commended the Anioma Watch Association for presenting mother-and-child starter packs to expectant women in the community as part of its ongoing antenatal outreach programme.


The initiative, held on Tuesday at the hospital, provided essential new-life care items to expectant mothers and marked the second community to benefit from the organisation’s latest outreach programme.


The Anioma Watch team, led by members of its Board of Trustees, had on Monday visited Ibusa, where expectant women from different ethnic and religious backgrounds also received similar support.


The Issele-Uku event opened with a prayer led by the Moderator of Pilgrim Baptist Hospital, Rev. Gabriel Ojji Okpala. Rev. Samuel Ugbaja, who welcomed the Anioma Watch delegation, provided an overview of the institution and introduced members of the hospital’s Board of Trustees.


In his remarks, the Chairman of the hospital’s Board of Trustees, Mr. Kingsley Azuh, thanked Anioma Watch for selecting the hospital as a beneficiary of its maternal-care initiative.


Azuh traced the history of the hospital to Rev. Martin Nwadei, an indigene of Issele-Uku who, after travelling to the United States, returned with ideas that contributed to the establishment of churches, schools and a hospital in the community.


He also credited Rev. Nwadei with establishing the structure of the technical school in Issele-Uku, which now serves as the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) Orientation Camp.


According to Azuh, Pilgrim Baptist Hospital once served as a major healthcare centre in Issele-Uku and neighbouring communities, providing quality medical services before experiencing a period of decline and abandonment. He said the facility was subsequently revived through the goodwill and intervention of concerned individuals.


Azuh expressed appreciation to Anioma Watch for choosing to support the hospital at a time when it needs assistance.


In his opening address, the Chairman of the Anioma Watch Board of Trustees, Dr. Emeka Esogbue, said the choice of Pilgrim Baptist Hospital was deliberate. He recalled that the organisation had previously visited the school arm of the institution, where it delivered a lecture on drug abuse prevention.


Esogbue urged the expectant women to raise their children in the fear of God, while encouraging them to embrace responsible parenting from the earliest stages of their children’s lives.


The President of Anioma Watch Association, Engr. Abela Emuebie, advised the women to maintain healthy diets appropriate for pregnancy and to follow the recommendations of their medical consultants.


Emuebie also assured the beneficiaries that Anioma Watch would continue to explore ways of supporting expectant mothers and families in the community.


The vote of thanks was delivered by the hospital’s Matron, Nurse Peace Michael Nwachukwu, who expressed gratitude to the Anioma Watch delegation for the gesture.


The event ended with a closing prayer led by Rev. Felix Ifeanyi Nwabuokei, Secretary of the Anioma Watch Board of Trustees.


Among those present were Rev. Gabriel Ojji Okpala, Moderator of Pilgrim Baptist Hospital; Mr. Kingsley Azuh, Chairman of the hospital’s Board of Trustees; Rev. Samuel Ugbaja, Secretary of the Board; Deaconess Patricia Chukwudi; Rev. Kingsley Onyekaonwu; and Nurse Peace Michael Nwachukwu, Matron.


Representing Anioma Watch were Miss Ifeyinwa Izegbu, Treasurer of the association, and Miss Joy Ozeh, Social/Welfare Secretary.

title: The Rare Picture of HRH Justina Okuakeleke Ntorka, the Last Omu of Onicha-Olona
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
The Rare Picture of HRH Justina Okuakeleke Ntorka, the Last Omu of Onicha-Olona




From the Pen Master Archives


Here is a rare picture of HRH Justina Okuakeleke Ntorka, the last Omu of Onicha-Olona, a woman whose name remains etched in the history and memory of the community.


Born Justina Monyei, she ceased to be known by that name following her coronation as the Omu of Onicha-Olona, assuming the royal identity and responsibilities that came with the revered stool.


Historically, Omu Ntorka succeeded HRH Ada Ifesimehone Amambiwemdi-Okoh, one of the most remembered Omus in the modern history of Onicha-Olona. Born in 1906 at Idumugbe, Ogbe-Obi, Omu Amambiwemdi-Okoh occupies a special place in the community's history, particularly for the role attributed to her during the Nigerian Civil War, an episode preserved not only in historical accounts but also in the enduring oral traditions and legends of the people.


With the planned installation of Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, the recent history of the Omu stool will be marked by three remarkable women: Amambiwemdi-Okoh, Ntorka and Jibunoh.


Yet, despite the significance of her reign, not many people outside Onicha-Olona have had the opportunity to see the face of Omu Justina Ntorka, the community's last Omu.


Today, Pen Master brings that rare piece of history to light.


A photograph, yes but also a window into the memory of a community, a royal institution, and a remarkable woman whose place in the story of Onicha-Olona deserves to be remembered.


For your news on Anioma communities, follow the "Pen Master" on Facebook.

title: Expectant Mothers in Ibusa Receive Essential Newborn Care Packs from Anioma Watch Association
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Expectant Mothers in Ibusa Receive Essential Newborn Care Packs from Anioma Watch Association






By Peter Oshagwu


Nearly 100 expectant mothers at the Ibusa Primary Health Care Centre, opposite St. Augustine’s Catholic Church, on Monday received essential mother-and-baby care packs donated by the Anioma Watch Association as part of its antenatal outreach programme.


The initiative, which brought excitement to the beneficiaries, was designed to support expectant mothers with basic supplies ahead of childbirth and promote responsible motherhood in the Ibusa community.


The event, which commenced at 11:00 a.m. with an opening prayer led by Miss Joy Ozeh, featured the introduction of members of the Anioma Watch Association, led by its President, Engr. Abela Emuebie.


Welcoming participants, the Chairman of the association’s Board of Trustees, Emeka Esogbue, explained that the New Life Care Pack was conceived to provide practical support to mothers preparing for childbirth.


Esogbue expressed satisfaction with the standard of care at the health centre, noting that residents had widely recommended the facility when the association sought an appropriate location for the outreach.


He particularly commended the Matron, Mrs. Obi Caroline Nneka, for what he described as her high level of professionalism and the confidence she had earned among patients.


Describing Anioma Watch as a regional watchdog committed to promoting the interests and development of Anioma communities, Esogbue urged the beneficiaries to contribute to the advancement of Ibusa and to remain committed to the wellbeing of their families and community.


The Omu of Ibusa, HRH Obi Josephine Nwannabuogwu, who attended the programme, praised Anioma Watch for extending its intervention to women, particularly expectant mothers in Ibusa.


She described the New Life Starter Pack as a valuable provision that would assist the women as they prepared for motherhood.


The traditional ruler also encouraged the women to approach her whenever they encountered communal challenges, assuring them of her willingness to listen and support them.


Addressing the expectant mothers, the Omu explained that pregnancy comes with significant biological and physical changes, stressing that such changes are a normal part of the journey to motherhood.


She urged the women to take the responsibility of raising their children seriously and provide them with proper training and guidance so they could grow into responsible and productive members of Ibusa society.


The President of Anioma Watch Association also appealed to the expectant mothers to pay close attention to their health and wellbeing during pregnancy, particularly in their choice of food and drinks.


The major highlight of the outreach was the presentation of customized bags containing essential items for mothers and newborn babies to the expectant mothers.


The gesture elicited excitement among the beneficiaries and staff of the health centre.


In her vote of thanks, the Matron, Mrs. Obi Caroline Nneka, expressed appreciation to Anioma Watch for selecting the facility for the outreach.


She described the intervention as significant, saying the volume of items presented to the expectant mothers was substantial and that the entire health centre was delighted by the gesture.


The programme ended with a closing prayer led by Rev. Felix Ifeanyi Nwabuokei, General Secretary of the Anioma Watch Association Board of Trustees.


Other Anioma Watch members present included Miss Ifeyinwa Izegbu, Treasurer, and Miss Joy Ozeh, Welfare/Social Secretary, alongside members of staff of the Ibusa Primary Health Care Centre.


The initiative was sponsored by USA-based Dr. Anthony Ezeagbor from the Issele-Uku community. Other communities to be visited are Issele-Uku, Onicha-Olona and Amai in Ukwuani Local Government Area of Delta State.

title: Omu Josephine Urges Ibusa Expectant Mothers to Raise Responsible Children
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Omu Josephine Urges Ibusa Expectant Mothers to Raise Responsible Children




By Emeka Esogbue


The Omu of Ibusa, HRH Obi Josephine Isioma Nwannabuogwu, has urged expectant mothers in the community to embrace the responsibility of raising children who will grow into responsible, productive and valuable members of Ibusa society.


Obi Josephine made the call while serving as Special Guest of Honour at an antenatal outreach programme organised by the Anioma Watch Association, a registered socio-cultural organisation of Anioma people, in Ibusa.


Speaking to the expectant mothers, the Omu acknowledged the biological and physical challenges that accompany pregnancy, noting that such changes are normal aspects of the journey to motherhood. She, however, stressed the importance of proper upbringing, training and guidance in shaping children into responsible members of society.


She encouraged the women to see motherhood as a major responsibility and to prepare themselves for the task of nurturing children who would contribute positively to the development and progress of Ibusa.


Obi Josephine also commended the Anioma Watch Association for choosing Ibusa from among several communities for the outreach, describing the gesture as a meaningful intervention for expectant mothers in the community.


The Anioma Watch Association, on Monday, presented New Life Starter Packs to expectant women at the Ibusa Primary Health Care Centre, located opposite St. Augustine's Catholic Church, Isieke.


Receiving the guests and the items on behalf of the health facility, the Matron, Mrs. Obi Caroline Nneka, expressed appreciation to the Anioma Watch Association for the initiative.


Mrs. Nneka described the gesture as significant to both the hospital and the beneficiaries who chose the facility for their antenatal care. She urged the expectant mothers to take matters concerning their health seriously and make proper use of available maternal healthcare services.


The outreach underscored the importance of community support for expectant mothers and the need to promote maternal and child welfare across Anioma communities.

title: Pen Master Unveils Photos of Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, Set to Emerge as New Omu of Onicha-Olona
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Pen Master Unveils Photos of Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, Set to Emerge as New Omu of Onicha-Olona





For the first time, Pen Master is unveiling photographs of Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, the woman widely favoured to succeed the late Omu Ntoka, the former Omu of Onicha-Olona, and assume the revered traditional leadership position of the community’s female institution.


The development follows recent efforts by the Onicha-Olona community to revive its female traditional institution after a six-year interregnum. In the course of the process, Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, an indigene of Idumu-Ozolumuna in the Ogbe-Obi axis of Onicha-Olona, has emerged as the leading candidate for the prestigious position.


Her anticipated emergence is significant, as the installation will restore continuity to an institution that has remained without an Omu for six years. If installed as expected, Jibunoh will become the latest Omu in the Anioma region, further underscoring the cultural importance of the occasion.


Pen Master presents three photographs of the woman at the centre of this historic development. The images capture her in both her pre-chalked and chalked states, offering readers a glimpse of the traditional rites and preparations associated with her impending installation.


The installation ceremony is scheduled to take place on August 28, 2026, in Onicha-Olona, where preparations are already gathering momentum ahead of the historic event.


As anticipation builds within and beyond the community, congratulatory messages have continued to pour in for Cynthia Nwamaka Jibunoh, her family, and the people of Onicha-Olona.


The expected installation promises to mark a new chapter in the history of the community’s female traditional institution and a significant moment in the preservation and renewal of Anioma cultural heritage.

title: When the Living Must Not Dance: The Sacred Dance of Ibusa's Ulor
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
When the Living Must Not Dance: The Sacred Dance of Ibusa's Ulor



By Emeka Esogbue


During the Ulor Festival celebrated by the Umueze Quarters of the Ibusa community, there comes a solemn and mysterious moment when a particular dance is performed, one to which the living, even those gathered within the festival arena, must never surrender their bodies. At this sacred hour, the drummers sit or stand with their drums firmly secured between their legs, beating the resonant instruments with their bare hands. Elderly men and other ritual characters summon from the drums a deep, solemn rhythm, while sonorous male voices carry a hauntingly beautiful chant into the air. Yet, beautiful as the music may be, the living must not dance to it.


This is a sacred dance offered to the ancestors, many of whom, while they walked the earth, once participated in the very festival now being celebrated in their honour. The music seems to belong to another realm: its melody is soulful, its rhythm hypnotic, and its chant almost otherworldly. The deep voices rise and fall over the resonant beats of the egede drums, while the akpele, the native flute, weaves its plaintive voice through the soundscape.


Not a nod of the head.

Not a tapping of the fingers.

Not the slightest movement of the feet.


Even when the rhythm becomes irresistible and the chant swells triumphantly with the sound of akpele native flute. With “Ogayo, Ogayo, Ogayo, Ogayo, Ogayo, Gayo, Gayo, Gayo Na Enu o”—the people remain rooted to their places. No one dares to yield his body to the music.


Here lies the profound symbolism of the ritual: the living must not only honour the dead; they must also give them their moment. The ancestors are not to be displaced, imitated, or overshadowed by the living. This is their dance, their hour, their sacred space. The living stand aside, acknowledging that the world of the departed possesses mysteries and privileges that must be approached with reverence.


Whereas the dance of the Iwu Festival celebrants imitates the legendary movements of spirits believed to have come from the spirit world, this particular aspect of the Ulor Festival reverses the order. Here, the living surrender the dance entirely to the spirits. They allow the ancestors to dance first, undisturbed and unchallenged.


The chant may swell until it seems to fill the entire head and stir the deepest recesses of the soul, yet the audience remains motionless. Indeed, to prevent anyone from mistaking the sacred performance for ordinary dance music, the people may be warned beforehand not to dance to it, a solemn admonition traditionally believed to protect the living from spiritual consequences.


They are glad they were informed beforehand. After all, to be forewarned is to be forearmed; hence, everyone quickly adjusts.


Only after these sacred rites have been observed, and the ancestors have been accorded their due, may the celebrants once again loosen their bodies and display their own dance steps.


Such is the ancient power accorded to the spirits over the living: even in the midst of celebration, there remains a boundary between the two worlds, a boundary marked not by walls, but by silence, stillness, reverence, and an enduring respect for those who came before.

title: Onicha-Olona to Install Nwamaka Jibunoh as the New Omu of the Community
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Onicha-Olona to Install Nwamaka Jibunoh as the New Omu of the Community



By Emeka Esogbue


All is set for the people of Onicha-Olona, an ancient Anioma community in Aniocha North Local Government Area of Delta State, to install Nwamaka Cynthia Jibunoh as the new Omu of the community.


The installation ceremony is scheduled to take place on August 28, 2026, at Umuozolumuna, Ogbe-Obi Quarters, Onicha-Olona.


In a message to the Ogbe-Obi family and the general public, the community called for collective prayers for the new Omu and expressed hope that her reign would usher in blessings, peace and greater development for Onicha-Olona.


The message also charged the incoming female traditional leader to deploy her leadership to advance the fortunes of the community and take Onicha-Olona to greater heights.


The installation will mark a new beginning since the passing of Omu Ntoka, the last Omu of the community. Before Omu Ntoka was Her Royal Highness Omu Ada Ifesimehone Amambiwemdi-Okoh.


Onicha-Olona settlement is among the Anioma communities with a longstanding tradition of Omu institution. The forthcoming installation is therefore expected to renew an important aspect of the community's traditional heritage and female leadership.


Omu Ifesimehone Amambiwemdi-Okoh remains an important figure in the history of Onicha-Olona. Born in 1906 and from Idumugbe, Ogbe-Obi, she is particularly remembered in community history for her role during the Nigerian Civil War.


Historical accounts credit the Omu with mobilising traditional leaders and confronting the threat posed by Federal troops approaching Onicha-Olona in 1967. Her intervention has since become part of the community's oral history and enduring traditional narrative.


Available accounts state that Omu Ifesimehone reigned from 1963 until 2007 and died that year at the age of 101. She was buried on October 13, 2007.


Her long reign and the reverence attached to her memory have given added significance to the return of the Omu institution to Onicha-Olona after the interregnum.


The emergence of Nwamaka Cynthia Jibunoh is thus being viewed not merely as the installation of a new traditional title holder, but as a renewal of an institution deeply embedded in the cultural history of Onicha-Olona and the wider Anioma people.


The August 28 ceremony is expected to attract members of the Ogbe-Obi family, traditional institutions, community leaders, sons and daughters of Onicha-Olona, as well as other guests from across Anioma.

title: The Local Meaning Behind Ibusa’s “High Street”
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
The Local Meaning Behind Ibusa’s “High Street”


By Emeka Esogbue

Pen Master


"Pen Master explains the English origin; Onowu Chuks Esogbue explains the local resonance."


After Pen Master (Emeka Esogbue) wrote his article on Ibusa’s Isieke High Street, titled “Isieke High Street, Ibusa: How an English Urban Concept Was Naturalized Within an Indigenous Settlement,” Onowu Chuks Esogbue followed up with a complementary contribution that enriches and deepens the account.


While Pen Master’s article establishes the linguistic and historical thesis that Isieke High Street represents an example of an English urban concept being absorbed, adapted, and naturalized within an indigenous Nigerian setting, Onowu Chuks Esogbue’s response takes the discussion further by offering local reasons why the appellation “High” may have been particularly apt for Isieke, beyond the conventional British meaning of High Street.


Onowu Chuks proposes that Isieke was “high” in several locally intelligible senses, foremost among them its geographical and civic centrality. According to his account, Isieke lies at the centre of Ibusa, where Otu Odogwu, Otu Uwolor, and Otu Iyase meet. This gives the word High a possible spatial and civic significance: Isieke was not merely another street within Ibusa but occupied a central position in the settlement and functioned as an important point of convergence.


This observation potentially strengthens Pen Master’s original argument. The expression High Street may have been borrowed from an English urban vocabulary, but its application to Isieke was not necessarily an arbitrary imitation of a British naming convention. The designation may have resonated with an existing local reality, one in which Isieke already occupied a position of geographical, social, and commercial prominence within Ibusa long before the name was conceived.


Viewed together, the two accounts therefore present Isieke High Street as more than a linguistic curiosity. They reveal how a borrowed English expression could be incorporated into an indigenous geographical vocabulary as the Ibusa people did while acquiring meanings rooted in the history and lived experience of the community itself.


In this sense, the “High” in Isieke High Street may be both English in origin and distinctly Ibusa in resonance, a fascinating example of linguistic adaptation, cultural appropriation, and local place-making.


Connected to other places of the world with the exact name, Isieke stands out among name-places in Ibusa. Curiously, the Ibusa children of tomorrow will inquire on the reason for the street name and the arguments of Chuks Esogbue will be offered. Isieke really lies at the intersection or convergence of important parts of Ibusa, this is highly relevant to its status as a principal street.


The presence of major entertainment and commercial establishments fits remarkably well with the conventional meaning of High Street. The missionary and Catholic history strengthens the argument that the street was a major public corridor. 


The historical value of Isieke's antiquity and prestige, particularly as the choice of European acceptance to establish a church is important but maybe not an explanation for High Street. Although Ibusa encountered an English urban concept and appropriated it to describe a street whose local importance made the concept meaningful, the community did not surrender the indigenous identity of the place. Isieke remains Isieke. English only supplied an additional descriptor. 


For linguists, the Ibusa example helps to explain a familiar phenomenon in language contact: communities do not merely receive foreign words passively. They select, reinterpret, combine and domesticate them.

title: Asaba Set to Immortalize 1967 Massacre Victims with Monumental Memorial
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Asaba Set to Immortalize 1967 Massacre Victims with Monumental Memorial


By Emeka Esogbue
Pen Master

Plans are underway in Asaba, the Delta State capital, to immortalize the victims of the October 1967 Asaba Massacre with a monumental memorial that will preserve their memory for generations to come.

The initiative features prominently among the priorities of His Royal Majesty, Prof. Epiphany Chigbogu Azinge, SAN, OON, the Asagba of Asaba, who has demonstrated a strong commitment to preserving the history, heritage and collective memory of the Asaba people.

As part of the initiative, internationally acclaimed artist and sculptor Mr. Enyi Echezona Jr., a multi-talented painter and sculptor of Anioma origin, has been approached to develop the proposed memorial. Echezona has already presented a proposal for the construction of a gigantic symbolic monument dedicated to the memory of those who lost their lives during the tragic events of October 1967.

The proposed monument is expected to serve not only as a memorial to the victims but also as an enduring historical landmark where present and future generations can learn about the tragedy and appreciate the resilience of the Asaba people.

Speaking on the initiative, the Asagba of Asaba acknowledged the painful history of the massacre and paid tribute to the remarkable resilience of the community in the aftermath of the tragedy.

The monarch particularly sal


uted the women of Asaba, many of whom, following the massacre and the loss of their husbands, were forced to assume the responsibilities of breadwinners and single-handedly raise their families. He described their strength, courage and sacrifices as an important part of the history and survival story of Asaba.

According to the monarch, the development witnessed in Asaba over the years stands as a testimony to the strength, resilience and determination of its people. He noted that the community has grown rapidly, particularly since it became the capital of Delta State, despite the painful experiences that shaped its history.

He stressed the importance of remembering the past while building a stronger and more prosperous future, noting that the proposed memorial would provide an opportunity to preserve the historical consciousness of the people.

Giving the public an insight into the proposed project, Echezona Jr. explained that the monument would stand approximately 45 feet tall and feature a lighthouse, mini gallery and mini museum. The names of the victims of the massacre would also be prominently displayed, providing visitors, researchers and tourists with an opportunity to engage with the history of the tragedy.

According to the artist, the project was conceived as a lasting tribute to the victims and as a means of ensuring that future generations never lose sight of the history and significance of the events of October 1967.

It is hoped that the proposed monument will complement the existing memorial artwork at Ogbeosowe in Asaba and further strengthen efforts to preserve the community's historical heritage.

Asaba is fortunate to have a traditional ruler who understands the importance of history and believes passionately in preserving the story of his people. The proposed monument is therefore more than a structure of art and architecture; it represents remembrance, honour, identity and a commitment to ensuring that the sacrifices of the past are never forgotten.

As Pen Master, I am particularly pleased to be part of this historic effort and honoured to work closely with the globally respected artist, Enyi Echezona Jr. towards preserving the memories, history and legacy of our people.

For Asaba, this is not simply about erecting a monument. It is about remembering the dead, honouring the survivors, celebrating the resilience of a people and educating generations yet unborn about a defining chapter in their history.

title: The Russia–Ukraine War: A Classroom in Post-WWII Diplomacy
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
The Russia–Ukraine War: A Classroom in Post-WWII Diplomacy


By Emeka Esogbue


As a passionate student of history and diplomacy, I have followed the Russia–Ukraine war with more than ordinary interest because, beyond the battlefield itself, the conflict has become a remarkable demonstration of how post-World War II diplomacy actually operates. What we studied in classrooms as theories of alliances, strategic partnerships, deterrence and balance of power is being played out in real time.


This makes sense to me more than the classroom explanations and illustrations by teachers. I am not listening to my lecturers or reading books on diplomacy but watching the conflict play out exactly the way a passionate student of the subject will understand it. Russia, China, North Korea, Ukraine, Turkey and the USA appear to be practicalizing the warfare for us, the students.


The war is, on the surface, a conventional conflict between Russia and Ukraine. But beneath that conventional warfare lies a much broader contest involving competing alliances, strategic interests and spheres of influence. It is almost as if the principles of international relations are being rehearsed on the battlefield for students of diplomacy to observe.


One of the most striking developments has been North Korea's increasingly direct support for Russia. Pyongyang has moved beyond diplomatic sympathy and has become materially involved in Moscow's war effort, including the provision of military personnel and weapons. North Korean forces have consequently gained something that the country's military has rarely possessed in modern times: significant contemporary battlefield experience. Recent reporting indicates that the scale of North Korean involvement could grow further.


China's relationship with Russia adds another important dimension. It would be historically inaccurate to call Russia, China and North Korea a revival of the old WWII "Axis"—that term properly refers to Germany, Italy and Japan. Nevertheless, the growing strategic convergence among Moscow, Beijing and Pyongyang is difficult to ignore. It represents an increasingly visible alignment of states that are challenging, in different ways, the political and security order dominated by the United States and its European and Asian partners.


What makes the present situation particularly interesting, however, is that the international system is not divided into two perfectly disciplined camps. Türkiye is a good example.


Türkiye has maintained a complicated relationship with Russia. Ankara has neither completely severed its relationship with Moscow nor abandoned its own strategic interests. At the same time, Türkiye has consistently supported Ukraine's sovereignty and defence capabilities. Its earlier provision of Bayraktar drones became one of the most recognizable examples of Turkish military assistance to Ukraine.


More recently, Türkiye has taken another significant step. In August 2026, the United States notified Congress of a proposed Turkish transfer of substantial American-origin weaponry to Ukraine: 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems, 70 M39 ATACMS missiles, 2,524 M26 rockets and 47,000 203-mm artillery rounds. The package is valued at roughly $280 million and is intended to strengthen Ukraine's offensive and defensive fire-support capabilities. Because some of these systems are of U.S. origin, the transfer requires the relevant American authorization process.


This is precisely why Türkiye's position is so important to the study of diplomacy. Ankara demonstrates that modern alliances are not always simple matters of "friend" and "enemy." A state can maintain dialogue and economic relations with one power while providing military assistance to that power's adversary. Türkiye is a NATO member, has deepened its defence relationship with other NATO allies, and at the same time has sought to preserve its ability to communicate with Moscow. The July 2026 NATO summit in Ankara itself reaffirmed both Türkiye's importance to the Alliance and the continued commitment of NATO members to Ukraine.


In that sense, the Russia–Ukraine war is teaching an important lesson about international politics: alliances are rarely based solely on friendship; they are built around interests, security calculations, geography, history and the perception of future threats.


The war is therefore much larger than a contest over territory in Ukraine. It is also a test of whether the existing international order can withstand attempts to redraw borders through force, and whether states can maintain strategic autonomy while operating within competing networks of power.


I am particularly interested in what Russia's eventual post-war position will look like. If the conflict continues to impose enormous human, economic and technological costs on Russia, the long-term consequences could be profound. Russia may emerge weakened economically, demographically and militarily, even if it succeeds in retaining some territorial gains. The danger for Moscow is that victory measured in territory could ultimately become a strategic defeat measured in national power.


North Korea presents an even more extreme illustration of what prolonged isolation and militarization can produce. I therefore see the current conflict as an important historical lesson: military power can win battles, but sustainable national power depends upon economic strength, alliances, technological capacity, institutions and international legitimacy.


For students of diplomacy, this war is perhaps one of the clearest contemporary demonstrations that the international system created after 1945 is not a static arrangement. It is being renegotiated—through negotiations, sanctions, military assistance, strategic partnerships and, tragically, through war itself.


The battlefield, in other words, has become a classroom for international relations.

title: Aunty Rosemary Adams, Miss Independence 1960, is 85 years today. God has indeed blessed this Nigerian beauty.
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Aunty Rosemary Adams, Miss Independence 1960, is 85 years today. God has indeed blessed this Nigerian beauty.






Since my childhood, I have loved and followed Aunty Rosemary as an enthusiast, journalist, and advocate of the Enuani people even when she was completely unaware of my existence.


I first encountered her through her character, “Ngozi,” in Adio Family, a family social drama broadcast by the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA). My father would always point at her on the screen and exclaim, “She is our Enuani sister!” I would watch her with fascination, over and over again.


A few years ago, as part of the team of the Organization for the Advancement of Anioma Culture, our crew visited her home to interview her. That memorable interview was subsequently published in Anioma Essence Magazine.


A few weeks ago, while in Onicha-Olona, I specifically appealed to my guide to take me to her family home. I was shown an upstairs building belonging to the family, a modest but deeply meaningful connection to the story of this remarkable woman.


When you meet Aunty Rosemary, one of the first things that strikes you is her enduring physical beauty, followed closely by her near-impeccable English and that sweet, melodious voice with which God has so richly blessed the Anioma people.


Today, I celebrate Rosemary Nkem Anieze-Adams, the Anioma and Nigerian beauty; a woman whose presence on our television screens left an enduring impression on generations of Nigerians.


Happy 85th birthday, Aunty Rosemary!


May the years ahead be graceful, fulfilling, and filled with good health, peace, and a sound mind. May your remarkable legacy continue to inspire generations.


Emeka Esogbue (Pen Master)

title: 16th Memorial Anniversary of Hon. High Chief William Ukadike Ikolodo
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Ibusa Legends of Yesteryears


16th Memorial Anniversary of Hon. High Chief William Ukadike Ikolodo



By Emeka Esogbue


Hon. High Chief William Ukadike Ikolodo was a distinguished Nigerian politician, traditional leader, businessman, and philanthropist from Ibusa in Delta State.


He served as a member of Nigeria's House of Representatives during the Second Republic (1979–1983), representing his constituency until the civilian administration was overthrown in the military coup of December 1983. Beyond politics, he held the revered traditional title of Uwolo of Ibusa, the community's traditional war leader, a position synonymous with courage, leadership, and the protection of communal interests.


High Chief Ikolodo was widely admired for his unwavering commitment to education and community development. He sponsored scholarships, assisted countless young people in securing employment, and invested generously in projects that improved the welfare of his people. His generosity, mentorship, and vision helped shape the lives of many individuals who later became leaders and professionals in their own right (Esogbue, 2023).


Hon. High Chief William Ukadike Ikolodo passed away on 7 August 2010 at the age of 74. Sixteen years after his passing, his legacy continues to resonate throughout Ibusa and the wider Anioma community. He is remembered not only for his remarkable contributions to politics and traditional leadership but also for his enduring spirit of philanthropy, selfless service, and dedication to the advancement of his people. His life remains an enduring evidence of purposeful leadership and community service, securing his place among the most influential figures in the modern history of Ibusa.

title: Unearthing the Ibusa Experience: Recovering an Overlooked History of the Nigerian Civil War
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Unearthing the Ibusa Experience: Recovering an Overlooked History of the Nigerian Civil War


By Emeka Esogbue


In the course of gathering primary source materials for the book, "The Nigerian Civil War: An Ibusa Perspective," this author, under the guidance of Joy Ozeh, undertook extensive fieldwork across Ibusa, conducting interviews with surviving veterans, eyewitnesses, and other individuals whose lives were directly shaped by the Nigerian Civil War. The objective was to preserve firsthand accounts that might otherwise be lost to history and to document the wartime experiences of the Ibusa community from the perspectives of those who lived through the conflict.


The historical investigation yielded a wealth of invaluable testimonies and personal recollections. Most of the individuals approached willingly shared their experiences, recognizing the importance of preserving their memories for future generations. However, two potential respondents declined to speak. Remarkably, despite the war having ended approximately twenty-six years earlier, they remained deeply fearful of discussing their experiences, believing that doing so might still expose them to unforeseen consequences. Their reluctance serves as a poignant reminder of the enduring psychological scars left by the conflict and illustrates how trauma can persist long after the cessation of hostilities.


The field investigation further revealed that Ibusa was one of the significant theatres of the Nigerian Civil War, suffering widespread destruction and immense human hardship. Although the full scale of the devastation may never be accurately quantified, the evidence gathered indicates that the community endured losses comparable in severity to those experienced by many other war-affected areas. The suffering of the people of Ibusa was profound and deserves a place within the broader historical narrative of the conflict.


This raises an important historical question: Why has the Ibusa experience remained relatively undocumented despite the magnitude of its suffering?


One explanation lies in Ibusa's geographical location. Situated adjacent to Asaba and occupying a strategic borderland position, Ibusa was exposed to some of the most devastating consequences of the war. Yet, unlike neighbouring Asaba, its experiences have received relatively little scholarly attention and are rarely featured prominently in historical accounts.


The reasons for this disparity are not difficult to identify. The concentrated violence of the Asaba Massacre, during which large numbers of civilians were assembled and executed in a single location, became one of the defining atrocities of the Nigerian Civil War. The scale and visibility of that event attracted considerable scholarly, journalistic, and international attention. Researchers and human rights scholars, including Professors Elizabeth Bird and Erin Baines, have devoted significant effort to documenting the Asaba Massacre, preserving survivors' testimonies, and ensuring that the tragedy occupies its rightful place in historical memory.


By contrast, the tragedy of Ibusa unfolded in a markedly different manner. Rather than a single catastrophic event, the people of Ibusa endured a prolonged and grinding ordeal marked by displacement, deprivation, fear, and survival in forest camps. Death came not only through direct violence but also through hunger, disease, exposure, and the relentless hardships of wartime existence. Such experiences are inherently more difficult to capture in a single dramatic narrative or headline than a mass execution occurring at one identifiable location. Consequently, the story of Ibusa has remained largely absent from mainstream scholarship and public memory.


Drawing upon extensive field interviews with surviving actors and eyewitnesses, The Nigerian Civil War: An Ibusa Perspective seeks to address this historical omission. The book brings together these invaluable primary testimonies, critically analyses them in comparison with existing documentary and archival sources, and synthesizes the evidence into a comprehensive account of Ibusa's wartime experience. In doing so, it aims not only to preserve the voices of those who lived through the conflict but also to restore Ibusa to its rightful place within the history of the Nigerian Civil War, ensuring that its story is documented, understood, and remembered alongside those of other communities that endured the devastating consequences of the war.

title: Isieke High Street, Ibusa: How an English Urban Concept Was Naturalized Within an Indigenous Settlement
author: Emeka Esogbue - The Pen Master
contentHtml:
Isieke High Street, Ibusa: How an English Urban Concept Was Naturalized Within an Indigenous Settlement


By Emeka Esogbue


Among the many streets that traverse the ancient town of Ibusa in Delta State, Nigeria, one name stands out as a subject of historical and linguistic curiosity: Isieke High Street. To many Nigerians, the expression “High Street” sounds unusual, as it is more commonly associated with Britain, where it traditionally refers to the principal commercial street of a town. Yet, in Ibusa, the name has long formed part of the community’s own geographical vocabulary.


Rather than being merely a colonial imprint, Isieke High Street appears to represent a locally embraced designation that combines an indigenous place name, Isieke, with the English urban concept of High Street. The name offers a fascinating example of how foreign linguistic elements can be absorbed, adapted, and given local meaning within an indigenous settlement. It reveals the interaction between British linguistic influence and African place-making traditions, demonstrating how communities can transform borrowed expressions into markers of their own identity.


Ibusa and the Historical Context of English Influence


Ibusa, an important Anioma community, is located in present-day Delta State, Nigeria’s South-South geopolitical zone. By the 1860s and 1870s, the Asaba–Ibusa axis was already known to European traders, explorers, and officials before the arrival of the first Church Missionary Society (CMS) missionaries in 1875.


Historian Elizabeth Isichei notes that Asaba’s location along the River Niger placed it in contact with Europeans for more than a century, with European records documenting aspects of its history long before formal missionary activities began. By the second half of the nineteenth century, the Asaba–Ibusa area had already experienced decades of interaction with English language, commerce, and British institutions. These historical circumstances created an environment in which English expressions could be encountered, adopted, and eventually localized by the community.


Within this context, the adoption of the term “High Street” in Ibusa demonstrates how global vocabulary could enter local usage without necessarily displacing indigenous identity.


Isieke: An Indigenous Place Name Within Ibusa


Isieke is a locality within Umuekea, one of the ten quarters, known locally as "ogbe," that make up Ibusa. Situated almost at the centre of the settlement, Isieke has produced many accomplished individuals whose contributions have extended beyond the community into national and international spheres.


Among the notable families associated with Isieke are the Chigbue family, a lineage recognized for its remarkable contributions to education, law, and public service. The family produced some of the earliest prominent lawyers from Ibusa and established a distinguished legal tradition within the community.


Two notable figures from this lineage were Justice Victor J. O. Chigbue and his son, Chief Chike Chigbue, SAN, OFR. Justice Chigbue, who hailed from the Isieke axis and descended from the Obi Tenu lineage, was a distinguished jurist who served as a Justice of the Court of Appeal and, at one point, as Acting Chief Judge of the old Kaduna State before his retirement in the late 1990s.


Chief Chike Chigbue, SAN, OFR, became one of the youngest and most celebrated Senior Advocates of Nigeria of his generation. He was involved in notable legal matters, including the Boni Haruna governance case and important civil rights arguments concerning passport seizures, before his untimely death in 2001.


Isieke also produced internationally recognized personalities such as Prof Emeritus Augustine Onwuyali Esogbue, a renowned NASA scientist whose achievements brought global recognition to Ibusa.


Oral Tradition and the Origins of Isieke


Much of the history surrounding Isieke is preserved through oral tradition rather than written documentation. According to a popular account, Madam Ekea’s children with Ezemese gave rise to different branches of the community. Alamuzo, the second son, was said to have fathered Oshe and Oluo. Oshe, the elder, became the ancestor of Isieke, while Oluo became the ancestor of Nkpanyala.


Isieke developed as a settlement characterized by houses arranged along a long, narrow road, with residential buildings traditionally lining both sides. It was also the choice of the British missionaries who established the first church, St. Augustine's Catholic mission in the area. Over time, modern shops, businesses, and commercial outlets have emerged along this route, reinforcing its role as an important corridor within the community.


The Uniqueness of Isieke High Street


When the phrase “High Street” is mentioned, attention usually turns to Britain, where the name is found in numerous towns and cities, including Oxford, Glasgow, and Bristol. The name is also found in Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the United States, and Hong Kong.


However, less widely known is the existence of Isieke High Street in Ibusa, Delta State, Nigeria. Although the precise year when the street acquired the name “High Street” remains uncertain, by the early 1980s the designation was already commonly used within the community.


This makes Isieke High Street a remarkable example of an African adaptation of a globally recognized street name. It demonstrates that “High Street” is not confined exclusively to British towns or European urban traditions but can also become part of the geographical identity of an indigenous African settlement.


Isieke High Street as a Toponymic Heritage


From a linguistic perspective, Isieke High Street is an odonym, which is a type of toponym referring specifically to a street name. The name combines two elements:


- Isieke — an indigenous place-name rooted in Ibusa’s local history and identity.


* High Street — an English urban street term historically associated with a town’s principal route.


Together, these elements form a unique cultural expression: Isieke High Street. Unlike a simple imitation of British naming practices, the name carries an indigenous geographical identity while incorporating an English linguistic element.


Isieke High Street is therefore more than a street designation. It is a cultural marker of an ancient Anioma settlement, preserving local memory while reflecting historical encounters with global influences. It stands as an example of how African communities have incorporated and transformed foreign vocabulary while maintaining their own identity and heritage.


In this sense, Isieke High Street represents not the replacement of indigenous tradition, but the creative blending of cultures — a local expression of a global language within the historic landscape of Ibusa.
